method: Actually read all current fields of every151–175 item, including all options, keys and rationales. Clinical keys generally remained defensible, but every item had an identified distractor, cue, task-boundary or source-specific problem. Patches were individually reasoned; no blanket rejection/pass rule was used.
limitations: Independent AI review, not clinician or psychometric validation.
Targeted new sources were retrieved as search-result excerpts; author must register the supplied topic sources and record actual access before final reference reconciliation.
No claim of exhaustive cross-bank semantic comparison or live-exam comparison.

items.assessment: Nurse preference, hesitation equals every refusal and relatives taking over are conspicuous wrong answers. Compare recognizable bereavement-support approaches; add direct perinatal-loss support.
issues: Nurse preference, hesitation equals every refusal and relatives taking over are conspicuous wrong answers. Compare recognizable bereavement-support approaches; add direct perinatal-loss support.

options: Describe keepsakes other families valued and encourage the client to select those
Record the current hesitation as a decline and provide the bereavement booklet
Explain the choices, explore concerns and allow the client time to decide
Ask the partner to choose the keepsakes so the client can rest
why: Other families’ experiences may inform discussion but should not prescribe what is meaningful for this client.
Uncertainty calls for information and space; it is not a settled refusal of the available choices.
Sensitive explanation and exploration support an informed personal choice without pressure.
The partner can support the client if desired, but should not replace the client’s preference by default.

items.assessment: Blame allocation and stop-thinking language are obviously nontherapeutic. Use plausible reassurance, remembrance and factual-review responses.
issues: Blame allocation and stop-thinking language are obviously nontherapeutic. Use plausible reassurance, remembrance and factual-review responses.

options: 'You are carrying a lot of guilt; tell me what you are thinking.'
'Families often wish they had acted differently; try to focus on the good memories.'
'You supported your parent for years; remembering that may help you set this aside.'
'Let us ask for a review of the timeline so we can decide whether the call mattered.'
why: Exploration acknowledges the distress without deciding uncertain causation.
Normalizing can help, but moving directly to positive memories may close discussion of the current guilt.
Past caregiving may be a strength, but advising the client to set guilt aside does not explore its meaning.
A factual discussion may be useful later; immediately making this an investigation bypasses the expressed emotion and cannot promise an answer.

items.assessment: Exclusive emotional focus and mandatory independence are implausible. Add immediate practical cues and compare helpful but less targeted responses.
issues: Exclusive emotional focus and mandatory independence are implausible. Add immediate practical cues and compare helpful but less targeted responses.

proposedChanges.stem: A client bereaved last week feels overwhelmed by meals, appointments and paperwork. They have eaten very little today and missed collecting a regular prescription. What should the nurse do first?
options: Offer a bereavement helpline and information about a local support group
Help the client develop a detailed schedule for the next several months
Invite the client to describe memories of the person who died
Identify immediate food and medication needs and available practical help
why: Bereavement services may help, but the unmet needs today require a more immediate practical plan.
A long planning task may add to current overload before basic needs are addressed.
Reminiscence can provide emotional support but does not resolve the stated immediate needs.
Prioritizing basic needs and feasible support makes the next steps manageable.

items.assessment: Generic SATA uses ethnicity and the nurse’s own religion as transparent errors. Give a real ritual-planning context and credible assumption errors.
issues: Generic SATA uses ethnicity and the nurse’s own religion as transparent errors. Give a real ritual-planning context and credible assumption errors.

proposedChanges.stem: After a death, a family asks for a bedside mourning ritual the nurse does not know. Some requested timing may conflict with arrangements already planned. Which actions support respectful care? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the family which parts of the ritual are most important to them
Explore feasible changes to the timing with the relevant team
Use the cultural reference guide to select the ritual on the family’s behalf
Explain specific constraints and ask about acceptable alternatives
Arrange the hospital’s usual faith representative to lead the ritual
why: The family’s own account establishes its priorities rather than assuming uniform practice.
Coordination may make the requested practice possible within care arrangements.
A guide can inform respectful questions but cannot establish this family’s choices.
Transparent discussion supports collaboration when the exact request cannot be met.
The usual representative may not fit this family’s beliefs; ask who they would want involved.

items.assessment: Marriage-obligation language, only a sheet and waiting for crisis are bad-intent or delay cues. Compare realistic caregiver interventions.
issues: Marriage-obligation language, only a sheet and waiting for crisis are bad-intent or delay cues. Compare realistic caregiver interventions.

options: Assess care demands, caregiver wellbeing and immediate options for relief
Review strategies for responding to common dementia behaviours
Help the spouse design a relaxation routine for the evening
Arrange an earlier review of the care recipient’s dementia treatment
why: Missed meals, poor sleep and feeling trapped warrant assessment of caregiver health, safety and practical relief.
Skills education may reduce some demands, but does not by itself establish whether the caregiver’s basic needs and safety are being met.
Relaxation may help sleep but cannot compensate for an unmanageable care workload.
The recipient’s treatment may need review, but the spouse’s own health and support needs also require direct assessment.

items.assessment: Every task back, withdrawal from decisions and lost productivity make the key uniquely humane. Compare credible role-adaptation approaches.
issues: Every task back, withdrawal from decisions and lost productivity make the key uniquely humane. Compare credible role-adaptation approaches.

options: Focus on regaining the former responsibilities before introducing different household roles
Explore valued roles and agree on achievable contributions with the family
Have relatives take over household planning while physical recovery continues
Set rehabilitation goals around the tasks the family most wants completed
why: Waiting for former roles to return can miss meaningful contributions that are possible now.
Client-valued, achievable participation supports identity and recovery within current limitations.
Temporary help may be needed, but automatically taking over planning can remove an ability the client retains.
Family needs matter, but goals must also reflect the client’s values, abilities and recovery plan.

items.assessment: Financial authority, family votes and nurse preference are not plausible competing counselling plans.
issues: Financial authority, family votes and nurse preference are not plausible competing counselling plans.

options: Include the main daily caregiver in counselling because they provide most practical support
Begin with a joint family session to resolve the disagreement about participation
Clarify the client’s preferred involvement and agree on what information may be shared
Ask the counsellor to choose participants according to likely treatment benefit
why: Practical support does not replace the capable client’s consent to counselling involvement.
A joint session may be useful if the client agrees, but should not be the default solution to their request for privacy.
Client-defined limits establish legitimate participation and information sharing.
Professional advice can help the client decide, but does not supersede their wishes.

items.assessment: Immediate secrecy promises and inferred culture are conspicuous. Compare family protection, team disclosure and client-preference clarification.
issues: Immediate secrecy promises and inferred culture are conspicuous. Compare family protection, team disclosure and client-preference clarification.

options: Agree to postpone the discussion until relatives feel ready to support it
Arrange a family meeting to decide how much information the client should receive
Ask the clinician to disclose the full diagnosis immediately to ensure openness
Explore family concerns and clarify the client’s information preferences with the team
why: Relatives’ readiness does not establish the capable client’s wishes about receiving information.
Family input may help, but the client should determine their own desired information and involvement.
Honesty matters, but first establish how the client wants information shared, including any wish to involve others or limit detail.
This respects concerns while keeping the capable client’s preferences central to informed communication.

items.assessment: Blame and proving absence of disagreement are cartoon questions. Compare resource assessment with relevant background data.
issues: Blame and proving absence of disagreement are cartoon questions. Compare resource assessment with relevant background data.

proposedChanges.stem: A family is preparing for new daily care responsibilities after a crisis. Which questions directly identify their coping strengths, available support or support gaps? Select all that apply.
options: 'Who could help when meals, appointments or other responsibilities become difficult?'
'What helped your family manage a major change before?'
'How many times has your relative been admitted to hospital this year?'
'What support would make the next few days manageable?'
'What is the current schedule of prescribed medicines?'
why: Potential helpers identify practical and emotional resources.
Previous effective coping can identify strengths to use again.
Admission history describes illness burden; it does not directly establish coping strengths or available help.
The family’s immediate needs identify gaps that support planning can address.
The medicine schedule describes care demands; it does not establish who can manage them or what support is missing.

items.assessment: Conditional support and describing staying as consent are plainly harmful distractors. Keep safety planning but compare plausible partial responses.
issues: Conditional support and describing staying as consent are plainly harmful distractors. Keep safety planning but compare plausible partial responses.

options: Focus the visit on transport and packing for a possible shelter move
Assess current danger and build a safety plan with acceptable resources
Arrange relationship counselling to work on communication with the partner
Provide emergency contact details and invite the client to return when ready
why: Leaving-related preparations may be useful if wanted, but must follow assessment of the client’s current risks, wishes and safe options.
Safety planning can help while the client remains in the relationship; tailor it to current danger and accessible support.
Joint relationship counselling is not an automatic response to coercion or violence and can compromise safety.
Contact information is helpful, but should not replace individualized risk assessment and planning now.

items.assessment: Always/private browser and asking the abusive partner telegraph the answer. Compare realistic unsafe communication assumptions and add a direct technology source.
issues: Always/private browser and asking the abusive partner telegraph the answer. Compare realistic unsafe communication assumptions and add a direct technology source.

options: Send a neutral-looking text containing the service telephone number
Email a resource attachment rather than sending a visible text message
Ask which device, contact method and resource format can be used safely
Provide web links and suggest deleting the browser history afterward
why: Even neutral messages can leave records or reveal contact through a monitored device.
Email can also be monitored; changing format does not establish safety.
The client’s knowledge of monitoring should guide a safer communication plan before sending material.
History deletion does not remove every trace and changes may be noticed; assess device safety rather than relying on this step.

items.assessment: Every distractor simply denies the relevance of control. Compare plausible interpretations using explicit lack of choice.
issues: Every distractor simply denies the relevance of control. Compare plausible interpretations using explicit lack of choice.

proposedChanges.stem: A client says a partner controls the money and cancels medical appointments despite the client asking to attend. The client says the partner has never hit them. Which interpretation best guides further assessment?
options: The pattern may be coercive control affecting autonomy and access to care
The pattern primarily reflects an agreed division of household responsibilities
The main difficulty is the client’s lack of knowledge about appointment systems
The absence of physical assault makes ordinary relationship conflict most likely
why: Unwanted control of resources and health-care access can be harmful without physical assault.
The client’s expressed wish to attend is being overridden, so agreement should not be assumed.
The account describes another person blocking access, rather than a stated scheduling-knowledge gap.
No injury does not exclude nonphysical abuse or the need for private safety assessment.

items.assessment: Never/automatic police reporting and advice against reporting are transparent. Present reasonable but potentially premature support routes.
issues: Never/automatic police reporting and advice against reporting are transparent. Present reasonable but potentially premature support routes.

options: Encourage a police report promptly so the client will not lose an opportunity to act
Ask whether a relative can help decide before explaining the reporting options
Arrange counselling first and return to discussion of reporting at a later visit
Explain choices and applicable limits, and support the client’s informed decision
why: Time-sensitive evidence options should be explained, but the nurse should not steer a capable adult into a decision without informed discussion.
A chosen supporter may help, but the client needs information and control over whom to involve.
Counselling can be valuable, but postponing information may narrow options the client is currently considering.
Clear options, relevant time considerations and actual reporting limits support agency; requirements depend on the circumstances and jurisdiction.

items.assessment: Family acceptance and public accusation are too obvious. Compare private safeguarding with recognizable but inadequate budget/family approaches; add economic-abuse source.
issues: Family acceptance and public accusation are too obvious. Compare private safeguarding with recognizable but inadequate budget/family approaches; add economic-abuse source.

options: Speak privately about the arrangement and the client’s wishes
Assess food access, current safety and the decision-making context
Start with a joint family budget meeting to clarify the spending
Offer appropriate safeguarding and community support options
Provide a household budget worksheet as the initial response to the concern
why: Privacy can help establish consent, control and concerns without another person influencing the account.
Immediate unmet food needs and ability to make decisions may require prompt support.
A joint meeting before private assessment may inhibit disclosure or increase risk when exploitation is possible.
Relevant resources can support safety and informed options while applicable duties are reviewed.
Budget education may be useful for a knowledge gap, but does not first address possible unauthorized control and insufficient food.

items.assessment: Ignoring fear, simultaneous commands and rigid timing make the key obvious. Compare practical bathing adaptations.
issues: Ignoring fear, simultaneous commands and rigid timing make the key obvious. Compare practical bathing adaptations.

options: Use a familiar caregiver, slower pacing and one-step explanations
Add a second familiar caregiver so the shower can be completed sooner
Demonstrate the entire shower sequence before beginning the usual routine
Schedule the shower at the usual time and offer a preferred activity afterward
why: The described trigger is rushed care and the client tolerates familiar routines; pacing and familiarity address that pattern.
Additional help may be needed for physical safety, but shortening the task does not necessarily reduce perceived threat from rushing.
A long demonstration may overload processing and leaves pacing during the actual care unchanged.
Consistency and a preferred activity may help, but do not directly address distress caused by how the shower is introduced and paced.

items.assessment: Admission of forgetting, a lecture and proof of theft are implausible therapeutic responses.
issues: Admission of forgetting, a lecture and proof of theft are implausible therapeutic responses.

options: Remind the client that staff documented where the purse was placed
Acknowledge the worry and help the client find the safely stored purse
Offer a familiar activity to draw attention away from the missing purse
Explain that memory changes can make safely stored belongings seem lost
why: The record may be accurate but does not necessarily reduce the client’s immediate insecurity.
Validation followed by locating the purse addresses the concern and provides concrete reassurance.
Redirection can sometimes help, but an accessible direct resolution is available here.
Education may help at another time, but can be harder to process than finding the item that is causing worry.

items.assessment: Waiting for agitation or a monthly review are obvious delays. Ask for interpretation among clinically relevant explanations.
issues: Waiting for agitation or a monthly review are obvious delays. Ask for interpretation among clinically relevant explanations.

proposedChanges.stem: A normally interactive resident with dementia becomes unusually quiet and inattentive over one shift. Which interpretation should guide the nurse’s next assessment?
options: Gradual dementia progression has reduced the resident’s need for interaction
Less agitation indicates that the existing behavioural-care plan is effective
An acute change from baseline may represent hypoactive delirium or illness
Fatigue is the likely explanation because the resident is less physically active
why: A change over one shift is not safely attributed to gradual progression.
Quiet behaviour with new inattention does not establish improvement.
Assess physiology, medicines, pain and other possible contributors and report the acute change; delirium can present with reduced activity.
Fatigue is a possibility, but does not justify overlooking acute cognitive change without assessment.

items.assessment: Personality judgement and louder commands are bad-intent distractors. Compare useful assessments or comfort actions while keeping post-fall injury priority.
issues: Personality judgement and louder commands are bad-intent distractors. Compare useful assessments or comfort actions while keeping post-fall injury priority.

options: Ask the familiar caregiver to describe behaviour during previous turning care
Use a calm familiar approach and offer a pause before the next turn
Review environmental triggers associated with distress during personal care
Assess for pain and injury using physical and observational findings
why: Baseline behaviour is useful, but the new change after a fall requires direct injury and pain assessment.
Calm pacing supports care, but should accompany rather than replace assessment of the post-fall symptoms.
Environmental triggers may contribute, but a physical injury is a more immediate concern with new guarding and grimacing after a fall.
Nonverbal behaviour may express pain; assess possible injury before treating this simply as care resistance.

items.assessment: Continuous darkness and repeated confrontation are giveaway extremes. Retain recognizable sleep/orientation technique errors with specific actions.
issues: Continuous darkness and repeated confrontation are giveaway extremes. Retain recognizable sleep/orientation technique errors with specific actions.

options: Use short calm orientation cues as tolerated
Make needed glasses and hearing aids available
Keep curtains closed throughout the daytime to extend opportunities for sleep
Offer familiar supportive contact suited to the client’s tolerance
Ask the client to repeat orientation answers until each response is accurate
why: Gentle repeated cues can support connection without overwhelming the client.
Sensory access can reduce avoidable misinterpretation and isolation.
Prolonged daytime darkness may disrupt sleep-wake cues rather than restore orientation.
Familiar contact can reduce fear and support communication while causes are treated.
Performance-style repetition can increase fatigue or distress; orientation is supportive care rather than a test the client must pass.

items.assessment: Punishment and pre-emptive restraint are implausible. Compare information relevant to different parts of a walking-safety plan.
issues: Punishment and pre-emptive restraint are implausible. Compare information relevant to different parts of a walking-safety plan.

proposedChanges.stem: A resident with dementia walks toward the exit each afternoon saying they must collect their children. Which information would be most useful for planning an individualized redirection strategy?
options: The resident’s former afternoon routines and the meaning of collecting the children
The resident’s current fall-risk score and usual walking distance
The location of the nearest exit and the daily visitor numbers
The most recent orientation score and errors about the current year
why: The timing and stated purpose can identify a familiar role or unmet need for a meaningful response.
Mobility risk matters for safety, but does not explain why this repeated activity occurs at this time.
Environmental safety matters, but traffic and exit distance do not establish the resident’s underlying concern.
Cognitive testing provides background but does not identify the meaning of this particular pattern.

items.assessment: All choices removed, every preference delegated and repeated complex tests are caricatures. Make choice formats the genuine alternatives.
issues: All choices removed, every preference delegated and repeated complex tests are caricatures. Make choice formats the genuine alternatives.

proposedChanges.stem: A client with dementia follows one-step requests and points to preferred clothing, but becomes distressed when the full wardrobe is opened for dressing. Which approach best preserves participation?
options: Lay out several complete outfits so all possibilities are visible together
Offer two suitable garments at a time and allow a simple choice
Use the outfit the client preferred yesterday to shorten the decision
Ask the client to rank clothing preferences on a written list
why: Too many simultaneous options repeat the observed source of overload.
A limited meaningful choice matches the client’s demonstrated ability and preserves current preference.
Past preferences can help, but should not automatically replace a choice the client can still make.
Ranking several written options adds processing demands beyond the one-step ability described.

items.assessment: Speed, louder instructions and avoiding all care are conspicuous. Compare plausible approach changes.
issues: Speed, louder instructions and avoiding all care are conspicuous. Compare plausible approach changes.

options: Give the full care explanation from the doorway before approaching the bed
Maintain a running explanation while beginning the hands-on care
Approach within view, identify oneself and explain before each contact
Ask a second caregiver to distract the resident with conversation during care
why: An explanation at a distance may not ensure recognition and readiness when contact occurs.
Narration after touch begins may not prevent the initial surprise that triggered the response.
Visible predictable contact directly addresses startle and perceived threat.
Distraction can help some care, but unexpected touch can remain frightening if approach and preparation are unchanged.

items.assessment: Public correction and repeated performance comparisons are obvious. Use recognizable well-intended memory strategies.
issues: Public correction and repeated performance comparisons are obvious. Use recognizable well-intended memory strategies.

options: Use shorter name-and-date quizzes so the client experiences more successful answers
Prepare the correct answers before visits and rehearse them together
Use a family photo album mainly to practise identifying each person
Choose conversation and activities that draw on the client’s remaining interests and abilities
why: Shorter tests can still turn visits into performance demands when repeated quizzing is already distressing.
Rehearsal may not restore lost memory and can displace enjoyable connection.
Photos may support connection, but using them mainly as a naming test can recreate frustration.
Strength-based interaction supports dignity and connection without requiring correct recall.

items.assessment: The original asks what to track: even worsening outcomes and time can be worth tracking, so the key is not exclusive. Ask which findings support effectiveness and use clinical outcomes.
issues: The original asks what to track: even worsening outcomes and time can be worth tracking, so the key is not exclusive. Ask which findings support effectiveness and use clinical outcomes.

proposedChanges.stem: A dementia-care team changes bathing time and uses a familiar caregiver to reduce distress while meeting hygiene needs. Which findings support effectiveness of the revised plan? Select all that apply.
options: Distress episodes during bathing are less frequent and less intense
The client participates in washing with a relaxed expression and fewer pauses
Baths finish faster, but grimacing and attempts to pull away have increased
Skin and hygiene needs are met using the revised approach
The client is quieter after sedating medicine but cannot participate in washing
why: Reduced distress supports the stated aim of the adaptation.
Comfortable participation demonstrates a useful functional response.
Speed does not establish benefit when distress has increased.
The plan must meet necessary physical-care goals as well as reduce distress.
Reduced activity after sedation does not establish comfortable participation or effectiveness of the bathing adaptation.

items.assessment: Intentional behaviour and memory exercises alone are transparent misconceptions. Use parallel clinical explanations.
issues: Intentional behaviour and memory exercises alone are transparent misconceptions. Use parallel clinical explanations.

options: Attention can fluctuate during delirium even while the underlying illness still needs treatment
The periods of clarity establish that the acute physical problem has resolved
The variation is best understood as steady progression of chronic memory loss
A correct orientation answer shows that difficulties following care instructions have ended
why: Fluctuation is a feature of delirium; repeat assessment and treatment of causes remain necessary.
A lucid interval does not establish recovery of the underlying acute illness.
Rapid fluctuation over hours differs from the usual slower course of chronic cognitive decline.
One correct response does not establish sustained attention or ability to follow a sequence.
